`nomgeo` turns the street addresses in US police records into latitude and longitude. It is
built for research that maps incidents to census geographies (blocks, block groups, tracts)
and runs entirely on your own [Nominatim](https://nominatim.org/) server, built from
[OpenStreetMap](https://www.openstreetmap.org/) (OSM) and US Census TIGER house-number ranges.

Police records are not postal addresses. Most give a hundred block (`1300 9TH ST`), an
intersection (`UNIVERSITY AVE & 7TH ST`) or only a street, they use local abbreviations, and
many are not addresses at all (`UNKNOWN`, highway ramps, other cities). `nomgeo` is designed
around four rules:

1. **Match against what exists.** Every record is compared with the streets, address points
   and house-number ranges stored in the database for the police department's area.
2. **No silent guesses.** A record is placed only where there is evidence for it. If two
   different places fit, it stays uncoded and the output says why.
3. **Every result says what it is:** a match type (house, block, intersection, ...), an
   estimated precision in metres, the street names that were matched, and which
   relaxations (typo, missing direction, ...) were needed.
4. **Fast and repeatable.** The same input, settings and data always give the same result.
   About 250,000 records from eight cities take under four minutes from scratch, about a
   minute after a rule change, and ten seconds when nothing changed.

Everything runs locally, so there are no usage limits or fees, and the records, which often
include victims' home addresses, never leave your machine.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Software used: Ubuntu 24.04, PostgreSQL 17.5 with PostGIS 3.5, Nominatim 5.1.0, Python 3.12,
the Geofabrik North America extract of May 2025, and Nominatim's preprocessed TIGER 2025
house-number data. The machine is a 6-core desktop with 64 GB RAM and an NVMe SSD.
:::

# Requirements and installation {#sec-install}

## Nominatim with TIGER data

`nomgeo` needs a standard Nominatim installation and nothing else. Follow the official
[installation manual](https://nominatim.org/release-docs/latest/admin/Installation/) and
import an OSM extract that covers your cities (North America, the US, or a single state;
a state extract is enough for one police department and fits on a laptop). Street geometry
is read from Nominatim's own tables, so no second database is needed.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check the planner statistics
PostgreSQL normally collects table statistics at the end of an import. Without them, lookups
on Nominatim's 23-million-row `word` table took 0.7 s instead of 0.07 ms on the machine
above, and the TIGER import below ran at 6 lines per second instead of about 1,900.
`SELECT relname, last_analyze, last_autoanalyze FROM pg_stat_user_tables;` shows whether they
exist, and `ANALYZE;` in the `nominatim` database creates them.
:::

Then add the US Census TIGER house-number ranges, which supply house numbers for streets
where OSM has none (see the [Nominatim TIGER guide](https://nominatim.org/release-docs/latest/customize/Tiger/)):

``` bash
cd /srv/nominatim/nominatim-project            # the Nominatim project directory
psql -d nominatim -c 'ANALYZE;'                # planner statistics, see the tip above
wget https://nominatim.org/data/tiger2025-nominatim-preprocessed.csv.tar.gz   # 1.9 GB
nominatim add-data --tiger-data tiger2025-nominatim-preprocessed.csv.tar.gz --threads 4
psql -d nominatim -c 'ANALYZE location_property_tiger;'
echo NOMINATIM_USE_US_TIGER_DATA=yes >> .env
nominatim refresh --functions
sudo systemctl restart nominatim
```

On the machine above the import took 5 hours for the whole country (34 million ranges) and
added 8.6 GB to the database. It is worth it: TIGER raises the match rate of the example
datasets from 75% to 86% (@sec-results).

## The Python package

``` bash
git clone https://github.com/hungkitwchiu/nominatim-geocoding.git
cd nominatim-geocoding
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
```

The database connection is set in `configs/defaults.yaml` (`database:`); the password can
also be given with the `NOMGEO_DB_PASSWORD` environment variable. A read-only PostgreSQL
role is sufficient.

# Quick start {#sec-quickstart}

A dataset is one CSV file of addresses (@sec-input) plus a small YAML file:

``` yaml
# configs/berkeley.yaml
name: berkeley
input: BER_address.csv
area:
  city: Berkeley                # city boundary, looked up in Nominatim
  state: CA
  bbox: [-122.34, 37.92, -122.20, 37.84]   # optional outer box: left, top, right, bottom
rules: configs/rules/berkeley.csv          # local name fixes (may be empty)
parsing:
  redacted_first_token: true    # Berkeley's "00" redaction, see @sec-config
```

``` bash
.venv/bin/python -m nomgeo run configs/berkeley.yaml          # one dataset
.venv/bin/python -m nomgeo run configs/*.yaml --jobs 5        # all of them
```

Each run writes `outputs/<name>/results.csv` (one row per unique address, in input
order), `outputs/<name>/unmatched.csv` (sorted by reason) and `outputs/<name>/summary.json`.
Join `results.csv` back to the original data on the `address` column.

To see how one record is read and matched:

``` bash
.venv/bin/python -m nomgeo explain configs/berkeley.yaml "UNIVERSITY AVE & 7TH ST, BERKELEY, CA"
```

``` default
UNIVERSITY AVE & 7TH ST, BERKELEY, CA
  parsed: kind=intersection number=None streets=['UNIVERSITY AVE', '7TH ST']
  candidates for 'UNIVERSITY AVE':
     pen=0 'University Avenue'     flags=[]  pieces=111 separate_streets=1
  candidates for '7TH ST':
     pen=0 'Seventh Street'        flags=[]  pieces=35 separate_streets=1
  result: {"status": "matched", "match_type": "intersection", "lat": 37.8682201,
           "lon": -122.2966514, "precision_m": 10, "matched": "University Avenue & Seventh Street",
           "source": "osm_geometry", "in_city": 1, "penalty": 0, "detail": "6 crossing point(s)"}
```

# Preparing the input {#sec-input}

The input is a CSV file with a column named `address` (another name can be set with
`address_column` in the dataset file), one record per row, in the form `street, city, state`:

``` default
address
"1300 9TH ST, BERKELEY, CA"
"UNIVERSITY AVE & 7TH ST, BERKELEY, CA"
"2900 BLOCK S 72ND ST, Lincoln, NE"
```

`results.csv` has one row per distinct `address`, with the text unchanged, so the column is
the key for joining the results back to the original records. Build it from the original
column without other edits; duplicates are removed automatically.

`nomgeo` understands the usual police conventions by itself:

* hundred-block numbers (`1300` = the 1300–1399 block) and real house numbers, detected per
  dataset;
* intersections written with `&`, `/`, `//`, `@`, `AT` or `AND`;
* `BLOCK` and `BLK`, units and notes (`APT 6`, `# 1`, `(REAR)`, `SUITE`), and travel
  directions on surface streets (`CORNHUSKER HWY EB`);
* street-type and direction abbreviations (USPS Publication 28), ordinals (`7TH` = Seventh),
  and `ST`/`MT`/`DR` at the start of a name (Saint, Mount, Doctor).

Other conventions should be converted before geocoding, or with a rule file (@sec-config):

``` default
"EDWARDS AV + WILLOW ST"     →  "EDWARDS AV & WILLOW ST"      other connectors
"205X SUMMIT AVE"            →  "2055 SUMMIT AVE"             masked digits
"[2900]-[3000] ALMADEN RD"   →  "2950 ALMADEN RD"             number ranges
"1300 9TH ST"                →  "1300 9TH ST, Berkeley, CA"   missing city and state
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Is the street in OSM?
Search for a street on [openstreetmap.org](https://www.openstreetmap.org/) to see whether
and how it is mapped. A street that is missing or misspelled there cannot be matched until
it is fixed (@sec-iterate).
:::

# How a record is matched {#sec-how}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: "From a raw record to a result. Every arrow into 'uncoded' carries a reason into unmatched.csv."
flowchart TD
  A["record<br/>1300 9TH ST, BERKELEY, CA"] --> B["parse and classify"]
  B -->|"ramp, placeholder, another city,<br/>coordinates, empty"| U1["uncoded, with reason"]
  B -->|"address, street, intersection, between"| C["resolve street names against<br/>the streets of the area"]
  C -->|"no street fits"| P["named-place search<br/>(place-like text only)"]
  C --> D1["house or block number<br/>OSM address points, TIGER and OSM ranges"]
  C --> D2["intersection<br/>crossing, or a near miss up to 100 m"]
  C --> D3["street only<br/>short streets only"]
  D1 --> E{"one place?<br/>precise enough?"}
  D2 --> E
  D3 --> E
  P --> E
  E -->|"yes"| M["matched: type, lat/lon,<br/>precision, names, flags"]
  E -->|"no"| U2["uncoded, with reason"]
```

## The search area {#sec-area}

Each dataset has a **core** (the city boundary, looked up in Nominatim) and an **outer
box** (the `bbox` in the dataset file, or the boundary's box plus `buffer_km`). All streets
in the outer box are loaded into memory once: for San Jose that is 57,000 street pieces,
20,000 distinct names, 395,000 OSM address points and 91,000 TIGER ranges. Building this
index takes about 40 seconds, most of it checking the TIGER ranges (@sec-locate); it is then
cached, and loading it again takes about a second.

Matches outside the core are kept but flagged `outside_city`. Three rules keep them from
displacing the city's own streets:

* when a record fits a place inside and a place outside the city, the place inside wins
  (`preferred_in_city`);
* when the least-relaxed reading lies outside the city, an in-city reading that needs a little
  more relaxation (up to 3 penalty points, such as a direction the record left out) wins:
  `400 34TH ST, Norfolk` is Norfolk's West 34th Street, not Virginia Beach's 34th Street;
* when the record's street exists inside the city, house-number evidence from a same-named
  street more than 300 m outside the city is not used: `1715 COMO AV, Saint Paul` goes to Como
  Avenue at the city line, never to Southeast Como Avenue in Minneapolis.

Incidents just across the city line (mutual aid, unincorporated pockets, the far side of a
border street) and records for streets that exist only in a neighbouring city (a Virginia
Beach record for Norfolk's Granby Street) are still placed, flagged. Filter on `in_city` if
your study area is the city itself.

## Reading the record {#sec-parse}

The parser cleans the text and decides what kind of record it is. It never decides which
street is meant; that is left to the next step, which knows the streets that exist.

| Kind | Example | Handling |
|---|---|---|
| address | `1300 9TH ST` | number + street |
| intersection | `UTOPIA PL & PEAK DR`, `A ST/B ST`, `X AT Y`, `@ X` | two streets (also `AND`, but `ROUGH AND READY RD` is tried as one name too) |
| between | `26TH & K-N ST` (Lincoln) | 26th St between K St and N St: the midpoint of the two corners |
| street | `PHILHOWER DR` | street only |
| highway | `FERN VALLEY RD W TO I65S`, `136 I65S`, `ASHBY AVE & I-80` | ramps, directions of travel, interstates: not geocoded (policy) |
| junk, empty | `UNKNOWN`, `, San Jose, CA`, `3100` | not geocoded |
| other place | `GRETNA, NE`, `NEW PORT RICHEY FL` | not geocoded |
| coordinates | `200 37.8697;-122.3197` | not geocoded (policy; can be switched on) |

Along the way it removes units and notes (`# 1`, `APT 6`, `(REAR)`, `SUITE`, a unit
number after the street type such as `UNIVERSITY AVE 211`), strips travel directions from
surface-street intersections (`CORNHUSKER HWY EB & N 23RD ST`), and recognises that
`7 ST E` is Seventh Street East rather than house 7 on "ST E".

## Finding the street {#sec-resolve}

Input names and OSM names go through the **same** normalisation: case, accents and
punctuation; the full USPS list of street types (Publication 28, Appendix C1) plus local
types such as Arch, Quay, Close and Chase; directions (`N` = North); ordinals (`7TH` =
Seventh, `TWENTY FIRST` = 21st); and `ST`/`MT`/`DR` at the start of a name (Saint, Mount,
Doctor). Each name is split into direction, name, type and trailing direction, and only
peeled apart when a name remains, so Lincoln's `N ST`, `O ST` and `W ST` stay streets named
N, O and W.

A record's street is then looked up in tiers. The first tier that finds anything wins, so
a looser rule is only used when every stricter one failed:

| Tier | Example (record → OSM) | Penalty |
|---|---|---:|
| exact name | `9TH ST` → Ninth Street | 0 |
| spacing | `VANDORN ST` → Van Dorn Street; `IVANWAY ST` → Ivan Way | 1 |
| extra type | `UNIVERSITY AVE ST` → University Avenue | 1 |
| type is part of the name | `PINE LAKE` → Pine Lake Road; `ROSA PARKS` → Rosa Parks Way | 1 |
| words after the type | `S 13TH ST ANTIQUES` → South 13th Street | +1 |
| redaction wildcard | `KAI00 AVE` → Kains Avenue (Berkeley) | 2 |
| truncated field | `SILVERCREEK VALL` → Silver Creek Valley Road (San Jose) | 2 |
| typo | `UNVIERSTIY AVE` → University Avenue (1–2 edits, digits must agree) | 3–5 |

Within a tier, a record's direction and street type are compared with each candidate:

* a **missing direction** (`5TH ST` when only N 5th St and S 5th St exist) keeps all
  directional variants, and the house number or the cross street decides;
* a **missing type** (`1800 UNIVERSITY`) keeps all types, likewise;
* a **different type** (`FONTANOSO RD` when only Fontanoso Way exists) is accepted only if
  that name has a single type in the area (`CORNHUSKER RD` = Cornhusker Highway and West
  Cornhusker Highway), so `PARK AV` in Saint Paul, where there is no Park Avenue but Park
  Street, Park Terrace, Park Circle and other types, stays uncoded;
* a **conflicting direction** (`S 56TH ST` vs North 56th Street) never matches.

Typo tolerance is only used for a name that does not exist in the area at all. If
`GORDON AV` exists but is refused (Norfolk has Gordon Street and Gordon Walk, so the type
cannot be guessed), a street one letter away ("Dordon Street") is not taken instead, and a
typo is never combined with a changed type.

Every relaxation is recorded as a flag (`direction_added`, `type_missing`, `typo_1`, ...)
and adds to the penalty; at most 6 is allowed per street.

## Placing the record {#sec-locate}

**House and block numbers.** Most police data use hundred-block numbers (`1300` means the
1300–1399 block; San Jose's `3550` means the 3500–3599 block), detected automatically per
dataset. The evidence, in order of preference:

1. OSM address points on that street within the block: their centre (outliers dropped), and
   their spread as the precision;
2. a TIGER or OSM house-number range covering the block: the middle of that part of the
   street;
3. the known numbers just below and above the block on the same street, interpolated
   along the street.

Real house numbers (Saint Paul) look for that exact number first, then a range containing
it, then the neighbouring numbers (`interpolated`), and only then the block. When there is
no evidence for the number, the record is placed only if the whole street is short (see
street-only below) and the street's own known numbers do not contradict it: `1400 MASON ST,
Cambridge` stays uncoded because Mason Street is numbered 4–18.

Nominatim's own search answers with the whole street when it does not know a house number;
`nomgeo` never does that silently. The evidence is checked before it is used:

* An OSM address point counts only if its own `addr:street` is the street it is attached to.
  Nominatim attaches a house to the nearest road when no street with its name is close,
  which would put, for example, Louisville's airport "Terminal Drive" numbers on Crittenden
  Drive. A moved or missing direction ("6th Street East" on East 6th Street) and small
  spelling differences are tolerated, but the street type must agree ("Sunnyhills Court"
  numbers do not count for Sunnyhills Drive). The spellings become alternative names of the
  street unless a real street elsewhere in the area already has that name. This also
  repairs typos in OSM itself: Norfolk's street is mapped as "O Connor Crescent" but its 367
  addresses say "Oconner Crescent", which is what the police write.
* A number with no `addr:street` at all counts only if its street is clearly the nearest
  (within 60 m and at least 10 m closer than any other street), not a corner lot between two.
* A TIGER range counts only if at least half of it runs within 30 m of a street with the
  same name as the one Nominatim attached it to; Nominatim falls back to the nearest road
  when names differ (0.8% of the ranges fail this check in Berkeley, 5.6% in Saint Paul).
* Evidence more than 150 m apart is treated as separate places. Long streets that cross town
  lines often restart their numbering: `0 MASSACHUSETTS AVE` has a 0–99 block in Boston,
  Cambridge and Arlington, and the one inside the city wins. Evidence for the same street
  within 400 m is one block (a long block whose few addresses sit at both ends). A lone
  stray point on the same stretch is ignored when four times as many points agree there,
  but an in-city place is never discarded in favour of one outside the city.

Candidate streets that still point to **different** places make the record ambiguous:
`700 LITTLE CREEK RD, Norfolk` stays uncoded because both East and West Little Creek Road
have a 700 block.

**Intersections.** The two streets' real geometries are intersected. Crossing points within
60 m of each other (divided roads, slip lanes) are one junction. If the same two streets cross
in two places more than 80 m apart (`MARTIN LUTHER KING JR WAY & ADELINE ST` in Berkeley
cross near Ashby BART and again at 63rd St), the record is ambiguous. Two streets within
15 m of each other count as meeting there (a junction drawn slightly apart, flag `small_gap`),
so a second such junction makes the record ambiguous too. Loop streets that OSM stores as
closed shapes are treated as their outline, so a crossing is never placed inside the loop.
Junctions on a motorway are interchanges and not geocoded.

If the streets do not touch but come within **100 m**, the record is a near miss
(`near_intersection`). That covers a junction drawn with a small gap (Berkeley's traffic
diverters) and the San Jose habit of recording a cul-de-sac with its nearest through street.
How the point is placed depends on how the two streets approach each other:

* one street ends at, or points to, the gap: the middle of the gap, precision gap/2 + 10 m
  (`PORTSWOOD CL & EARLSWOOD CT`, gap 81 m, 51 m);
* a short street runs beside the other one (a cul-de-sac parallel to the avenue): the middle
  of that stretch, precision √((gap/2)² + (stretch/2)²) + 10 m, flag `side_by_side`
  (`EDEN AV & ONYX CT`, an 89 m court 92 m from the avenue, 74 m);
* the two streets run side by side for more than 100 m (`near_side_by_side_max_m`): **not a
  near miss**. Two parallel streets a block apart have no particular closest point, so
  `WARD ST & DERBY ST` in Berkeley (84 m apart) and `KENNEDY AV & NEWTON AV` in San Jose
  (81 m) stay uncoded.

When the exactly-named streets do not meet, one more attempt is made with names one letter
away (`second_chance`), accepted only if those streets actually cross. The large search box
makes this necessary: Cambridge's `BRATTLE ST & HAWTHORNE ST` names Hawthorn Street, while
streets spelled "Hawthorne" exist only in neighbouring towns.

**Street only.** A record with just a street name is placed at the middle of the street,
but only when the whole street lies within 125 m of that point; long streets stay uncoded.
Weak relaxations (a changed type, a two-letter typo) are not accepted here, because nothing
else confirms them.

**Named places.** Only when no street of that name exists in the area, text that is not a
street (`FRESH POND GOLF COURSE`, `PORTER SQ`, `SENNOTT PARK`) is searched in Nominatim
within the area. A street that exists is never swapped for a place sharing its name:
`500 BROADWAY, Cambridge` is not the Broadway subway stop in Boston, and `400 GILMAN,
Berkeley` is not the "924 Gilman" club. A result is used only if it is called what the record
says (or the record spells out its full multi-word name), it is the only such place, and it
is small enough (radius ≤ 150 m; Danehy Park in Cambridge, 400 m across, and Fresh Pond Golf
Course, 650 m, are refused). Text that looks like a street name is never sent to this
search, so `LEIGHTON ST` cannot match "Leighton Street Car Wash", and on an intersection the
place must lie within 150 m of the other street (a "VTA Park and Ride" 16 km from Snell
Avenue is refused).

**Final checks.** A location with an estimated precision worse than 250 m is not accepted
(`evidence too imprecise`).

# Output {#sec-output}

`results.csv` has one row per unique input address:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `address` | the input text (join key) |
| `status` | `matched` or `unmatched` |
| `match_type` | see the table below |
| `lat`, `lon` | WGS84 coordinates |
| `precision_m` | estimated radius in metres within which the incident location lies |
| `matched` | the OSM street names (or place name) used |
| `source` | `osm_address`, `tiger`, `osm_interpolation`, `osm_geometry` or `nominatim` |
| `flags` | relaxations and notes, separated by `;` (below) |
| `reason` | for unmatched records: why |
| `kind` | the record kind from the parser |
| `in_city` | 1 if the point lies inside the city boundary |
| `penalty` | total relaxation (0 = exact) |
| `detail` | the evidence, e.g. `6 address point(s) in 1300-1399` or `gap 23 m` |

| Match type | Placed at | Typical precision |
|---|---|---|
| `house` | an OSM address point with that exact number | 15 m |
| `interpolated` | an exact number within a TIGER/OSM range or between neighbours | 25–40 m |
| `block` | the centre of a hundred block | 30–120 m |
| `between` | the middle of a street between two cross streets (Lincoln) | 50–180 m |
| `intersection` | where the two streets cross | 10 m |
| `near_intersection` | the middle of a gap of up to 100 m between the two streets | 15–60 m (up to ~80 m beside a cul-de-sac) |
| `street` | the middle of a short street (street-only records) | 25–125 m |
| `poi` | a small named place | 25–150 m |
| `coordinates` | coordinates typed into the record (only with `accept.coordinates_in_text`) | as typed |

Common flags: `direction_added` / `direction_dropped` / `direction_moved`,
`type_missing` / `type_changed` / `type_unreliable`, `spacing`, `typo_1` / `typo_2`,
`truncated`, `redacted_ordinal` / `redacted_name` / `redacted_zero_block`, `alt_name` (matched
an alternative or old OSM name), `unit_removed`, `outside_city`, `preferred_in_city`,
`number_not_found` (a short street was used because the number is not on it),
`block_of_exact_number`, `between_known_numbers`, `offset_of_intersection` (San Jose
`VINE ST S & O GOODYEAR ST`, "on Vine St south of Goodyear": precision at least 100 m),
`second_chance`, `side_by_side` (a near miss beside a short street), `small_gap` (streets
drawn up to 15 m apart at a junction), `trailing_text`,
`poi_side`, `outlier_points_dropped`.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Using precision in an analysis
Filter or weight on `precision_m` and `match_type` rather than on `status` alone. For a
census-block analysis a sensible starting point is to keep everything with
`precision_m <= 100`, and to check how sensitive the results are to including the rest.
:::

# Configuration {#sec-config}

`configs/defaults.yaml` holds everything that decides what counts as a match. A dataset
file can override any key.

| Key | Default | Meaning |
|---|---:|---|
| `numbering` | `auto` | `hundred_block`, `exact`, or `auto` (≥ 80% of numbers end in 00 or 50) |
| `precision.near_intersection_max_gap_m` | 100 | two streets this close count as meeting (@sec-decisions) |
| `precision.near_side_by_side_max_m` | 100 | ...unless they run side by side for longer than this |
| `precision.intersection_merge_m` | 60 | crossing points this close are one junction |
| `precision.ambiguity_radius_m` | 80 | candidate places within this radius are one place |
| `precision.street_max_radius_m` | 125 | street-only records: the street must fit in this radius |
| `precision.poi_max_radius_m` | 150 | larger named places are refused |
| `precision.same_street_merge_m` | 400 | evidence for one block on the same street within this distance is one place |
| `precision.max_precision_m` | 250 | nothing vaguer is accepted |
| `precision.fuzzy_min_length` | 5 | no typo tolerance for shorter names |
| `precision.max_penalty` | 6 | most relaxation allowed per street |
| `accept.street_only`, `accept.poi` | true | geocode these when unambiguous |
| `accept.highway_interchange`, `accept.coordinates_in_text` | false | ramps/interchanges and typed coordinates |
| `accept.outside_core` | true | keep matches outside the city boundary (flagged) |

The defaults target census **block and block-group** analysis, with near misses allowed up to
100 m because each carries its own precision. For tract-level work, loosening
`near_side_by_side_max_m` (see @sec-decisions) and `street_max_radius_m`
recovers more records at a known cost in precision.

Dataset-specific parsing options:

| Option | Used by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `strip_after: [";"]` | Lincoln | cut notes appended after a delimiter |
| `truncation_length: 30` | San Jose | the records management system cuts long fields; allow prefix matches on the last street |
| `redacted_first_token: true` | Berkeley | the first token had its last two characters replaced by `00` (`6700 ST` = 67th St, `KAI00` = Kains, `00 DARTMOUTH` = the 0–99 block) |
| `single_letter_suffixes: true` | San Jose | `OLIVE L` = Olive Lane; off elsewhere because Lincoln has an L Street |
| `between_hyphen: true` | Lincoln | `26TH & K-N ST` = 26th St between K and N |
| `unreliable_types: [ST]` | Lincoln | the department writes ST for streets of any type (`HUNTINGTON ST` = Huntington Avenue) |

**Rule files** (`configs/rules/<city>.csv`) hold local spellings, one rule per row with the
columns `match,replace,notes`. Matches are whole words and case-insensitive, regular
expressions are allowed, `no-boundary` in the notes allows partial words, and lines starting
with `#` are comments. Each file applies only to its own dataset. Street types, directions
and other generic abbreviations are handled in code, so a rule file only needs what is
particular to the city:

``` default
match,replace,notes
M L KING JR,MARTIN LUTHER KING JR,Berkeley name
STCLAIR,SAINT CLAIR,Saint Paul name
NEW AUTUMN ST,N AUTUMN ST,San Jose name/typo
VA BEACH,VIRGINIA BEACH,Norfolk abbreviation
```

# Working through unmatched records {#sec-iterate}

Every unmatched record comes with a reason, and many can be fixed:

1. `outputs/<name>/unmatched.csv` is sorted by reason, so a whole class of problems shows
   up together (`street not found: OCONNER CRES` ×22).
2. `python -m nomgeo explain <config> "<address>"` shows how the record was read, which
   streets were considered with which penalties, and the final decision.
3. Fix it in the narrowest place: a row in the dataset's rule file for a local spelling,
   a parsing option for a department-wide convention, the code for something general.
4. Re-run. Only that dataset's records are matched again, which takes seconds.
5. Add the case to `tests/regression_cases.csv` with the expected outcome, so a later
   change cannot quietly undo it, and run the tests:
   `python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .`

Some records will never match, and should not: other cities, `UNKNOWN`, a highway with
no cross street, a street that exists in neither OSM nor TIGER. If a street is missing or
misspelled in OSM, it can be fixed at [openstreetmap.org](https://www.openstreetmap.org/);
the fix reaches your database with the next data update (@sec-speed).

# Speed and caching {#sec-speed}

Three caches, all under `cache/`, each invalidated automatically:

| Cache | Holds | Reused until |
|---|---|---|
| `areas/*.pkl` | the street index of an area (streets, address points, number ranges) | the database data or the indexing code changes |
| `results.sqlite` | the final result of every record | the record, any setting or rule, the matching code, or the data changes |
| `nominatim.sqlite` | raw Nominatim answers (boundaries, named places) | the data changes |

The data version combines the OSM import date with the identity of the TIGER table, so a
data update clears everything that depends on it. The results cache is also keyed on the
area (box, city boundary, data and indexing code), and a failed city-boundary lookup stops the
run instead of silently matching without the city. Records that hit an error (a crash, a
Nominatim outage) are not cached and are retried on the next run. `--no-cache` ignores the
caches.

The caches clean up after themselves: per dataset they keep the street indexes and the
results of the three most recently used versions (so going back to the previous rules is
still instant) and delete older ones. Deleting `cache/` is always safe; it is rebuilt on the
next run.

Run times for the eight example datasets, measured with
`python -m nomgeo benchmark configs/*.yaml --jobs 5` (which empties the caches first) on the
machine described at the top:

{{< include _generated/timing.md >}}

A run from scratch is mostly spent building the street indexes, which happens again only
when the data or the indexing code changes. Only city boundaries and named places are
looked up through Nominatim's search; everything else is matched in memory.

**Updating the data.** Nominatim can be kept current with `nominatim replication` (see the
Nominatim manual). The caches notice the new data version by themselves.

# Example: eight police datasets {#sec-results}

The tables below come from running `nomgeo` with the default settings on address records
from eight US police departments. Saint Paul records real house numbers and the others
hundred blocks. Intersections make up a quarter to a half of the records, except in Norfolk,
where nearly all records are addresses; Lincoln also writes "between" records
(`26TH & K-N ST`).

{{< include _generated/results.md >}}

**What the TIGER data adds.** The same eight datasets matched with OSM data only, and with
the TIGER house-number ranges added:

| City | Records | Matched, OSM only | Matched, with TIGER | Gained | Matches using TIGER numbers |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Berkeley | 3,996 | 3,774 (94.4%) | 3,797 (95.0%) | +23 | 99 |
| Cambridge | 3,519 | 2,959 (84.1%) | 2,995 (85.1%) | +36 | 67 |
| Lincoln | 40,568 | 25,215 (62.2%) | 34,474 (85.0%) | +9,259 | 11,883 |
| Louisville | 43,919 | 37,348 (85.0%) | 37,951 (86.4%) | +603 | 1,059 |
| Norfolk | 12,395 | 10,734 (86.6%) | 11,198 (90.3%) | +464 | 903 |
| Saint Paul | 43,567 | 25,582 (58.7%) | 40,759 (93.6%) | +15,177 | 25,210 |
| San Jose | 67,470 | 53,382 (79.1%) | 54,428 (80.7%) | +1,046 | 2,040 |
| Virginia Beach | 33,763 | 28,859 (85.5%) | 29,438 (87.2%) | +579 | 936 |
| **All** | **249,197** | **187,853 (75.4%)** | **215,040 (86.3%)** | **+27,187** | **42,197** |

TIGER matters most where OSM has few building addresses: the search areas of Lincoln and
Saint Paul have 37,000 and 58,000 OSM address points, against 320,000 to 395,000 around
Louisville, Norfolk, San Jose and Virginia Beach. There it lifts the match rate by 23 and
35 percentage points; elsewhere by 0.6 to 3.7.

# Choices and limitations {#sec-decisions}

**How close is "near" for two streets that do not touch?** This is the setting with the
largest effect. San Jose records often name a cul-de-sac with its nearest through street,
which can be 80–200 m away. Near misses are accepted up to 100 m, each with its own
precision (gap/2 + 10 m); with a 40 m limit, 1,693 of San Jose's 2,106 near intersections
would stay uncoded. Near misses by gap:

{{< include _generated/near.md >}}

Streets that run side by side are never near misses, at any gap (@sec-locate). The first
column after the total below counts such pairs within 100 m of each other. In a sample of 200
of San Jose's, half ran side by side for over 250 m (truly parallel), and a quarter for
100–150 m. Raising `near_side_by_side_max_m` to 150 m would add that quarter at about 85 m
precision.

{{< include _generated/gap_tradeoff.md >}}

**Hundred-block numbers** are placed at the middle of the block. The incident could be
anywhere on the block, on either side of the street; `precision_m` reflects the block's
length. Census blocks are bounded by streets, so a point on a block face can belong to the
blocks on either side: for block-level analysis consider assigning such records to both
neighbouring blocks, or weighting them.

**Not geocoded by design:** highway ramps and interchanges, directions of travel, and
interstate mile markers (Louisville writes `136 I65S`; OSM has only 5 mile markers there,
so state DOT milepost data would be needed); typed coordinates (can be switched on).

**Coverage.** A street missing from OSM cannot be matched even if TIGER knows it, because
TIGER ranges are attached to OSM streets. Number evidence is best where OSM has building
addresses (Berkeley, San Jose) and relies on TIGER elsewhere.

**One area per dataset.** Each dataset is matched within one search area. For records from
several cities, make one dataset per city (split the input by city and state); each city's
street index is built once and then cached.

# Files {#sec-files}

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| `nomgeo/parse.py` | record kinds, cleaning, units, numbers, dataset conventions |
| `nomgeo/normalize.py` | name normalisation shared by records and OSM names |
| `nomgeo/streets.py` | the per-area street index built from `placex` and the number tables |
| `nomgeo/resolve.py` | street lookup tiers and penalties |
| `nomgeo/locate.py` | numbers, intersections, street-only, ambiguity |
| `nomgeo/nominatim.py` | named-place search with validation |
| `nomgeo/area.py`, `nomgeo/cache.py` | the search area and city boundary; the caches |
| `nomgeo/pipeline.py`, `nomgeo/cli.py` | batch run, outputs, `run` / `explain` / `benchmark` / `report` |
| `nomgeo/report.py`, `nomgeo/benchmark.py` | the tables on this page; run-time measurement |
| `configs/` | defaults, one file per dataset, rule files |
| `tests/` | unit tests and regression cases |
| `legacy/` | the earlier two-pass scripts (@sec-changelog) |

# Changelog {#sec-changelog}

## 0.1.0 (2026-10-24)

First release of `nomgeo`. It replaces the two-pass scripts `geocode.py` and
`geocode_pass2.py`, which are kept in `legacy/` with their
[documentation](https://hungkitwchiu.github.io/doc.geocode.html); their last version is
tagged `two-pass-final`.

For users of the two-pass scripts:

* Address files are used as before. The city-specific rows of `name_cleanup_rules.csv` and
  the boxes of `city_viewboxes.csv` moved to `configs/rules/<city>.csv` and
  `configs/<city>.yaml`; generic abbreviations are handled in code. The Saint Paul rule
  `STRYKER → Saint Ryker` was dropped (the street is Stryker Avenue).
* The separate `osm_raw` (osm2pgsql) database is no longer needed.
* The output columns are new (@sec-output).
* Results from the two-pass scripts should be re-checked before use. In samples of 300
  matches per city, 52–82% were not placed at the address but at the centre of one
  arbitrary piece of the named street (Nominatim's answer when it does not know a house
  number), up to 4 km away in Berkeley. Also: the "false intersection" buffer of `500` was
  applied to longitude/latitude, i.e. 500 degrees, so it had no distance limit; street names
  were matched as substrings (`7th St` matched 27th St, and Lincoln's lettered streets almost
  anything); only the first street of an intersection was limited to the city's box; empty
  or number-only records returned the city centre; and cleanup rules applied to every city
  (`A → Avenue` broke Lincoln's lettered streets). With the old output files listed under
  `legacy:` in a dataset file, `python -m nomgeo compare <config>` writes
  `outputs/<name>/compare_disagreements.csv`: the records the two place more than 250 m
  apart, or that `nomgeo` leaves uncoded.
